about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report (GAO-08-1138, issued September 17, 2008) is a follow-up audit of the Department of Health and Human Services' Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology. It updates whether HHS has defined and implemented an overall privacy approach for protecting electronic personal health information exchanged within a nationwide health information network, as GAO recommended in January 2007.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: GAO found that HHS fulfilled the first part of GAO's earlier recommendation by identifying milestones and assigning responsibility for integrating the outcomes of its privacy-related initiatives, and that it has taken important steps toward the other two parts. HHS and the Office of the National Coordinator continued initiatives, including use cases, network prototypes and trial implementations, standards harmonization, certification criteria, state-level collaborations, and advisory group recommendations, that address aspects of HIPAA privacy principles and challenges to exchanging electronic health information. However, GAO found that HHS has not fully implemented its recommendation because the department has not defined a process for ensuring that all privacy principles and challenges will be fully and adequately addressed. Without such a process, GAO concluded, HHS faces the risk that privacy protection measures may not be consistently and effectively built into health IT programs, potentially jeopardizing patient privacy and public confidence and trust.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: A September 2007 survey sponsored by the Institute of Medicine indicated that nearly 60 percent of respondents did not believe that the privacy of personal medical records and health information was adequately protected by federal and state laws and organizational practices. In April 2004, President Bush issued an executive order calling for widespread adoption of interoperable electronic health records within 10 years. In 2005, HHS awarded four health IT contracts that included requirements for developing solutions to comply with federal privacy requirements and identifying techniques and standards for securing health information. In January 2007, four test network implementations demonstrated potential nationwide health information exchange. HHS awarded contracts to nine health information exchange organizations and cooperative agreements to six additional organizations to develop trial implementations. The Secretary released a federal health IT strategic plan in June 2008, and the Office of the National Coordinator expected to publish a confidentiality, privacy, and security framework by December 2008. One strategy in the plan was to address inconsistent statutes or regulations for the exchange of electronic health information by the end of 2011. The State-Level Health Information Exchange Consensus Project issued a report in February 2007 and another report in March 2008. The Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security Workgroup submitted recommendations related to the notice principle in February and April 2008. The State Alliance for e-Health's information protection task force proposed five recommendations in August 2007. The audit was conducted from April 2008 through September 2008.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of Health and Human Services direct the National Coordinator for Health IT to include in the department's overall privacy approach a process for assessing and prioritizing its many privacy-related initiatives and the needs of stakeholders, to ensure that key privacy principles and challenges are fully and adequately addressed. HHS generally agreed with the information in the report but neither agreed nor disagreed with this recommendation.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that HHS has not fully implemented an overall privacy approach and that more work remains. It notes that HHS has not defined a process for ensuring that all privacy principles and challenges will be fully and adequately addressed, so some principles and challenges may receive extensive attention while others may receive inadequate attention. Recommendations from the Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security Workgroup and the National Committee on Vital and Health Statistics were still under consideration by the Secretary. The confidentiality, privacy, and security framework was expected to be developed and published by the end of calendar year 2008 but had not yet been completed as of the report. HHS's written comments also caution that the report lists representative examples of HHS initiatives and is not intended to provide a complete compilation of HHS's privacy and security activities.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: The report is addressed to the Chairman of the Subcommittee on Oversight of Government Management, the Federal Workforce, and the District of Columbia, Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, U.S. Senate, with copies sent to interested congressional committees and the Secretary of HHS.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This June 13, 2008 report by the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO-08-684), prepared for congressional committees, examines the status of property conveyances and transfers of administrative jurisdiction between the District of Columbia and the federal government under Public Law 109-396. It covers the steps taken and remaining to complete the conveyances, the limited development that has occurred and current land-use plans, and the challenges the District and federal government face, with particular attention to Poplar Point and Reservation 13.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's own findings are that no property conveyances between the District of Columbia and the federal government had occurred as of June 6, 2008, although all transfers of administrative jurisdiction became effective on December 15, 2006. The District and federal government have taken several steps toward completing the conveyances, but negotiations over cleanup, contamination testing, disagreement over Boathouse Row land, and the need to agree on an AOC property have slowed or delayed completion. Limited development has occurred on the exchanged properties, and development will take many years because plans for most sites must still be developed. The report also identifies challenges including cleanup uncertainties at Poplar Point, the transition of the Deputy Mayor's office to a development-coordination role, and reaching community agreement about development.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: No conveyances had occurred as of June 6, 2008, and all transfers of administrative jurisdiction became effective December 15, 2006. The two largest properties to be conveyed to the District are Poplar Point, a 110-acre property, and Reservation 13, a 67-acre property. A 2003 GAO report estimated that the District's structural fiscal imbalance likely exceeded $470 million annually and could have been as high as $1.1 billion; the cost of delivering an average level of services per capita exceeded the average state fiscal system by approximately 75 percent, or $2.3 billion more annually, and was over one third more than New York's. The Master Developer's vision for Poplar Point includes 1.5 million square feet of office space, 3.8 million square feet of residential units, 405,000 square feet of retail space, 70 acres of parks, a waterfront entertainment district, a deck over I-295, and an option for a soccer stadium. Reservation 13 plans call for about 3,000 new units of housing, nearly 5.5 million square feet of mixed-use development, and more than $80 million in new infrastructure upgrades. The current NPS and U.S. Park Police facilities at Poplar Point encompass 100,000 square feet and sit on approximately 18 acres. Commercial and residential development of Poplar Point is not likely to begin until 2011 and may take up to a decade. The AOC is to receive not more than 12 acres of District property, and GSA is to receive five buildings on the West Campus of St. Elizabeths. DMPED staffing increased from 33 full-time equivalents in September 2007 to 63 in June 2008 and was expected to grow to 73 by August 2008.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report does not settle the extent and location of cleanup required at Poplar Point, the cost of environmental cleanup, or the determination of responsibility for paying for it. It states that the amount of construction allowed before the Secretary of the Interior certifies replacement facilities are ready is unclear, and that NPS lawyers were examining the definition of 'construction project.' The exact boundaries of the Boathouse Row property to be conveyed had not been resolved. The report also notes that the completion date for District-GSA conveyances is uncertain, that AOC site identification was not close to completion, and that it was probably too early to tell whether the District's current development-management structure would be effective.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: The report is addressed to the congressional committees specified in the mandate: the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs and the House Committees on Oversight and Government Reform, Energy and Commerce, Natural Resources, and Transportation and Infrastructure, with copies sent to the Administrator of General Services, the Architect of the Capitol, the Secretary of the Interior, and the Mayor of the District of Columbia.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a September 10, 2008, U.S. Government Accountability Office report to congressional committees (GAO-08-773) on the Department of Defense's National Security Personnel System (NSPS). It assesses the extent to which DOD has implemented internal safeguards and accountability mechanisms to make NSPS fair, effective, and credible, and how DOD civilian employees perceive NSPS and what DOD has done about those perceptions, based on reviews of regulations and guidance, 12 installation site visits, DOD's 2006 and 2007 Status of Forces Surveys, and employee discussion groups.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: GAO found that DOD had taken some steps to implement all nine safeguards examined, but implementation of three safeguards could be improved immediately: DOD cannot determine before ratings are finalized whether results are nondiscriminatory because it does not require third-party predecisional analysis of rating results for anomalies; employees at some installations lack transparency over final results because DOD does not require commands to publish rating and share distributions, and 3 of the 12 sites visited did not publish them; and NSPS guidance that most employees should be rated as a "3" may discourage meaningful distinctions, with pay pool panel members acknowledging hesitancy to award ratings in other categories. GAO also found that NSPS employees were more positive than other DOD employees about some performance-management goals, such as pay raises depending on performance, but attitudes of employees with the most NSPS experience declined from May 2006 to May 2007, and discussion groups surfaced widespread concerns about morale, time burden, writing skills influencing ratings, lack of pay pool transparency, and rapid implementation. DOD did not have a specific action plan to address these generally negative employee perceptions.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: As of May 2008, 182,630 DOD civilian employees had been phased into NSPS, and approximately 273,000 employees remained to be phased in. DOD received over 58,000 comments during the NSPS design phase. A contract workshop used 95 experienced employees, and approximately 14 percent, or 71,000 employees, responded to a Web-based questionnaire. Training included a 10-hour employee course, 18 hours of basic training and 24 hours of pay pool panel training for managers and supervisors, 10 hours for employees, and 26 or more hours for human resource practitioners. DOD's November 2005 cost estimate was $158 million for fiscal years 2005 through 2008, and DOD estimated approximately $143 million in implementation costs for fiscal years 2009 through 2011. In the May 2007 Status of Forces Survey, an estimated 43 percent of NSPS employees compared with an estimated 25 percent of all other DOD employees said pay raises depend on how well employees perform their jobs. Among spiral 1.1 employees, the estimated percentage who agreed their performance appraisal was a fair reflection of performance declined from 67 percent in May 2006 to 52 percent in May 2007, and the estimated percentage who believed NSPS would have a positive effect on DOD's personnel practices declined from 40 percent in May 2006 to 23 percent in May 2007. The estimated percentage saying NSPS was worse than previous personnel systems rose from 44 percent in November 2006 to 50 percent in May 2007. DOD-wide rating distributions were 0.2 percent at rating 1, 1.6 percent at rating 2, 57.0 percent at rating 3, 36.1 percent at rating 4, and 5.1 percent at rating 5, and 9 of the pay pools visited had 60 percent or more of employees rated at the "3" level.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that DOD require a third party to perform predecisional demographic and other analysis as appropriate for pay pools, require overall final rating results to be published, encourage pay pools and supervisors to use all categories of ratings as appropriate, and develop and implement a specific action plan to address employee perceptions of NSPS ascertained from DOD's surveys and employee focus groups, including actions to mitigate concerns such as the potential influence of writing skills on ratings. DOD concurred with the recommendation to publish final rating results, partially concurred with the recommendations on using all rating categories and on the action plan, and did not concur with the recommendation for third-party predecisional analysis.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that it could not determine whether final rating distributions were meaningful because GAO did not have specific knowledge of employees' performance within pay pools; that employee survey responses were fairly evenly distributed across disagree, agree, and neither responses, so the overall trend and whether the negative movement would continue could not be known until employees had more time under NSPS and additional surveys were administered; that information from discussion groups is not generalizable to the entire DOD civilian population; that DOD's survey methodology was generally conducted in accordance with standard research practices but had some areas that could be improved; that DOD has not developed a new timeline for phasing in the remaining approximately 273,000 employees; and that DOD did not have a specific action plan to address negative employee perceptions, with PEO officials saying they wanted employees to have more time under the system before making changes.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report (GAO-08-852) examines the Department of Homeland Security's risk-based methodology for allocating Homeland Security Grant Program funds, focusing on how the methodology changed from fiscal year 2007 to fiscal year 2008 and how reasonable the fiscal year 2008 methodology is. It covers the Urban Areas Security Initiative and the State Homeland Security Program, the shift to metropolitan statistical area boundaries for urban areas, and limitations in the vulnerability element of DHS's risk analysis model.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The findings are GAO's own. DHS is primarily following the same methodology in fiscal year 2008 that it used in fiscal year 2007, with the principal change being the use of metropolitan statistical areas to define urban area boundaries. DHS's risk-based methodology is generally reasonable, but the vulnerability element of the risk analysis model has limitations that reduce its value: DHS assigned every state and urban area a vulnerability score of 1.0, so as a practical matter final risk scores are determined by the threat and consequences scores. DHS officials expanded the eligible urban areas in fiscal year 2008 to a total of 60 UASI grantees, in part to address the effects of the MSA change and to ensure all urban areas receiving fiscal year 2007 funding continued to receive funding. The report also observes that DHS could take an additional step to evaluate the reliability and validity of the peer review process.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Since 2002, DHS has distributed almost $20 billion in federal funding through various DHS grant programs. In fiscal year 2007, DHS provided approximately $1.7 billion to states and urban areas through the Homeland Security Grant Program, and planned to distribute approximately $1.6 billion under this program in fiscal year 2008. DHS used the same risk-based methodology to allocate $852 million in fiscal year 2008 under the Infrastructure Protection Program, according to DHS. In the risk analysis model, the Threat Index accounted for 20 percent of the total risk score, and the Vulnerability and Consequences Index accounted for 80 percent. The four consequence indices were: Population Index, 40 percent; Economic Index, 20 percent; National Infrastructure Index, 15 percent; and National Security Index, 5 percent. DHS assigned vulnerability a constant value of 1.0 across all states and urban areas. In fiscal year 2008, 60 UASI areas were eligible: the 7 Tier 1 UASI grantees received 55 percent of available funds, approximately $429.9 million, and the 53 Tier 2 UASI grantees received 45 percent, approximately $351.7 million. In fiscal year 2007, 45 candidates were eligible: the 6 Tier 1 UASI grantees were allocated approximately $410.8 million, or 55 percent, and the 39 Tier 2 UASI grantees received approximately $336.1 million, or 45 percent. The change to MSAs increased the total area of urban area footprints by almost 162,000 square miles. The statutory minimum for SHSP in fiscal year 2008 was 0.375 percent of total funds appropriated for SHSP. DHS assessed risk for the Census Bureau's 100 largest MSAs, as required by the 9/11 Act.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: GAO recommends that the Secretary of DHS instruct FEMA, I&A, and NPPD — the DHS components each responsible for aspects of the risk-based methodology used to allocate funds under the Homeland Security Grant Program — to formulate a method to measure vulnerability in a way that captures variations across states and urban areas, and apply this vulnerability measure in future iterations of this risk-based grant allocation model. FEMA and I&A concurred with this recommendation. The briefing in Appendix I also states that DHS could take an additional step to evaluate the reliability and validity of the peer review process.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report does not settle how vulnerability should be measured; it says DHS needs to formulate a method and apply it in future iterations. It states that DHS's constant vulnerability score of 1.0 ignores geographic differences in the social, built, and natural environments across states and urban areas. The report notes inherent uncertainty in information used for risk assessments and that assumptions and policy judgments are inevitable. It states that DHS did not provide details on what criteria its 'best fit' comparison of footprint alternatives was based on. It also notes that DHS's analysis of peer review results did not apply a generally-accepted method to ensure inter-rater reliability, and DHS identified resource constraints as a reason for not measuring inter-rater reliability. Earlier DHS acknowledged it did not have sufficient data on all infrastructures to know what specific vulnerabilities existed, and that fully developing the capability would require substantial time and resource investment. The report also notes that states without officials with sufficient security clearances will receive an unclassified version of their threat assessment for the fiscal year 2009 grant process, and currently threat assessments are transmitted only to DHS state representatives and state officials.

audience.text: It is a GAO report to the Chairman and Ranking Minority Member of the Subcommittee on Homeland Security of the Senate and House Committees on Appropriations, supporting congressional review of DHS's Homeland Security Grant Program risk-based grant methodology and allocations.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report, GAO-08-877, issued August 15, 2008, examining how the Department of Defense and the military services are managing the acquisition of tactical radio systems. The audit, requested by the Subcommittee on Air and Land Forces of the House Committee on Armed Services, looked at how planned investments in key tactical radio systems changed over fiscal years 2003 through 2007, why those changes occurred, and what challenges the services face in planning future tactical radio investments, particularly for the Joint Tactical Radio System (JTRS) and legacy radios.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's main finding is that DOD's tactical radio investments over fiscal years 2003 through 2007 shifted dramatically in size and composition: planned spending of about $3.2 billion became actual spending of about $8.3 billion, with about $5.7 billion going to legacy radios and about $2.5 billion to JTRS development, and no JTRS networking radios were produced or fielded during that period. The change was caused primarily by delays in JTRS development and production and by urgent demands for additional legacy radios from combat operations and force modernization. The report also finds that supplemental funding supplied most, an estimated $5.5 billion, of the additional funds, that the notification/waiver process did not effectively track tactical radio investments, that JTRS still faces technology, security, and cost challenges, that the services have scaled back planned JTRS purchases, and that DOD lacks a comprehensive strategy for balancing near-term and long-term tactical radio investments.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report states that DOD spent an estimated $12 billion on tactical radios over the last 5 years, comparable to the Army's Future Combat Systems ($10.4 billion) and the Navy's Virginia Class submarines ($10.8 billion) in the same period. Planned spending on JTRS and Army and Marine Corps legacy radios for fiscal years 2003 through 2007 was about $3.2 billion, while actual spending was about $8.3 billion; of this, about $5.7 billion was spent on legacy radios and $2.5 billion on JTRS development. The Army and Marine Corps planned to spend about $235 million on legacy radios; the Army planned about $140 million and the Marine Corps about $98 million. Actual legacy spending was about $5.7 billion, about 24 times what was planned, including Army spending of about $4.1 billion ($2.3 billion on SINCGARS and $1.8 billion on handheld and manpack radios) and Marine Corps spending of $1.6 billion. Supplemental funding supplied an estimated 90 percent, $5.5 billion out of $6.1 billion, of Army and Marine Corps legacy radio procurement funding between 2003 and 2007. The JTRS development cost estimate increased from about $3.5 billion to almost $6 billion through fiscal year 2011. The first JTRS Ground Mobile Radios were delayed 5 years, from 2005 to 2010. A legacy vehicle radio costs about $20,000, while its JTRS replacement is estimated to cost up to 10 times more; the average cost of the 4-channel JTRS Ground Mobile Radio is about $220,000, and the average unit cost of the 2-channel airborne JTRS radio is about $480,000. The AN/ARC-210 radio costs about $80,000, with most aircraft configured with two radios. The Army's authorized acquisition objective for SINCGARS rose from about 232,000 receiver/transmitter units in fiscal year 2002 to more than 526,000 in fiscal year 2007, and the Army bought 244,780 SINCGARS between 2003 and 2007. JTRS planned procurement quantities fell from 436,600 initially to 193,103 currently, including Ground Mobile Radios reduced from 108,086 to 86,512 and Handheld, Manpack, and Small Form Fit radios reduced from 328,514 to 95,551. The Army requested funds for 170,756 more SINCGARS when only 56,000 were needed, an overstatement of $1.7 billion. The report also includes costs of about $310 million for Army helicopter alternate radios, about $50 million for AN/ARC-210 modernization research and development, and about $868 million to retrofit and fully integrate JTRS networking capabilities into four Naval aircraft.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of Defense develop a comprehensive strategy and implementation plan for making sound investment decisions for tactical radios that is based on operational architectures defining battlefield communications and networking functions, assesses and prioritizes near- and long-term capability needs, sets bounds for the funding committed to address these needs, lays out an effective migration and fielding plan, and identifies contingencies in case of further JTRS problems and delays. The report also recommends that the Secretary of Defense reinvigorate the tactical radio notification/waiver process to provide department-wide insight into continued procurement of legacy and interim radios, with consideration given to ensuring clear guidance and procedures are developed and communicated across the department. The Department of Defense agreed with both recommendations.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that significant JTRS technological challenges remain, particularly size, weight, power, and thermal constraints and security architecture requirements, and that whether these challenges can be overcome will not be known until major test and evaluation events occur in the next few years. It notes that the security architecture of JTRS radios raised concerns not fully appreciated when the program began, and that security certification requirements remain a significant risk. The report also states that the 2003 joint migration plan has not been updated, that most service migration plans are outdated or incomplete, that services' input for a new fielding plan has not been linked to operational architectures and has lacked sufficient detail, and that a comprehensive plan balancing needs with resources is still lacking. It notes that the Army and Marine Corps' $3.3 billion supplemental request for fiscal year 2008 was not acted on by Congress, and that the Army overstated its SINCGARS funding request by $1.7 billion. The report also states that GAO was unable to obtain tactical radio investment plans or actual procurement information from the Navy or Air Force because those services do not centrally procure radios.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: The report is addressed to the Chairman and Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Air and Land Forces of the House Committee on Armed Services, and it also supports congressional oversight and DOD acquisition decisions, with copies sent to other congressional committees, the Secretary of Defense, the Secretaries of the Air Force, Army, and Navy, and the Director of the Office of Management and Budget.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report, GAO-08-976, issued September 2008, on the Veterans Health Administration's use of miscellaneous obligations. It reviews how VHA used miscellaneous obligations in fiscal year 2007 and whether VA's policies and procedures were designed to provide adequate controls over the authorization and use of these obligations, focusing on approximately $6.9 billion in miscellaneous obligations made by VHA's 129 stations during fiscal year 2007.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's own findings are that VHA used miscellaneous obligations extensively in fiscal year 2007 to record estimated obligations for mission-related goods and services, with over $6.9 billion recorded according to IFCAP data. The report found that VA policies and procedures were not designed to provide adequate controls over miscellaneous obligations in three areas: oversight by contracting officials, segregation of duties, and supporting documentation. These control design flaws were confirmed in case studies at Pittsburgh, Cheyenne, and Kansas City, and the report concludes they increase the risk of fraud, waste, and abuse. The report also found that new guidance issued in May 2008 offered some improvement but did not fully address the three problem areas, and that VA attorneys had not reviewed these policies.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: In fiscal year 2007, IFCAP data show that nearly 132,000 miscellaneous obligations with a total value of nearly $9.8 billion were created, including $6.9 billion by VHA's 129 stations and $2.9 billion by VA's Central Office. Of the VHA total, almost $3.8 billion, or 55.1 percent, was for fee-based medical and dental services, and another $1.4 billion, or 20.4 percent, was for drugs, medicines, and hospital supplies. In the case studies, 42 miscellaneous obligations totaling $36,045,896 were reviewed: 42 had no documented approval by contracting officials, 30 had inadequate segregation of duties, 8 had incomplete purpose descriptions, 20 had blank vendor fields, and 16 had blank contract fields. The IFCAP analysis identified 145 miscellaneous obligations for over $30.2 million that appeared to be used to procure items such as passenger vehicles, furniture and fixtures, office equipment, and medical, dental, and scientific equipment. Over 88,000, or 69 percent, of 127,070 miscellaneous obligations did not include vendor information, accounting for over $5 billion of the $6.9 billion in recorded miscellaneous obligations in fiscal year 2007.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of Veterans Affairs, in conjunction with VA's Office of General Counsel, develop and implement policies and procedures consistent with federal appropriations law and internal control standards that establish a process for the review of miscellaneous obligations by contracting officials, including requiring appropriate documentation that the review has occurred; segregate duties for creating, approving, and recording miscellaneous obligations, certifying and paying invoices, and receiving resulting goods or services; document the purposes, vendors, and contract numbers of miscellaneous obligations; and establish an oversight mechanism to ensure that these control policies and procedures are fully and effectively implemented. The report notes that VA concurred with these recommendations and identified specific actions it planned to take.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that GAO could not reconcile IFCAP miscellaneous obligations to VA's Financial Management System because FMS does not identify the method used to obligate funds. GAO did not review VHA's procurement or service authorization processes. The case study results were based on a nongeneralizable sample and cannot be projected to the overall population of miscellaneous obligations. GAO did not verify that VHA officials were properly following the Medicare fee schedule formula. The report found no examples of fraudulent or otherwise improper purchases, but states the work was not specifically designed to identify such cases or estimate their full extent. The report also notes that the May 2008 guidance did not fully address the identified control design flaws and that VA policies and procedures had not been subject to legal review.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: This report is addressed to the Chairman and Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations, Committee on Veterans' Affairs, House of Representatives, who requested the review, and was also sent to other interested congressional committees and affected federal agencies.

{
  "about": "This GAO report (GAO-08-1138, issued September 17, 2008) is a follow-up audit of the Department of Health and Human Services' Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology. It updates whether HHS has defined and implemented an overall privacy approach for protecting electronic personal health information exchanged within a nationwide health information network, as GAO recommended in January 2007.",
  "findings": "GAO found that HHS fulfilled the first part of GAO's earlier recommendation by identifying milestones and assigning responsibility for integrating the outcomes of its privacy-related initiatives, and that it has taken important steps toward the other two parts. HHS and the Office of the National Coordinator continued initiatives, including use cases, network prototypes and trial implementations, standards harmonization, certification criteria, state-level collaborations, and advisory group recommendations, that address aspects of HIPAA privacy principles and challenges to exchanging electronic health information. However, GAO found that HHS has not fully implemented its recommendation because the department has not defined a process for ensuring that all privacy principles and challenges will be fully and adequately addressed. Without such a process, GAO concluded, HHS faces the risk that privacy protection measures may not be consistently and effectively built into health IT programs, potentially jeopardizing patient privacy and public confidence and trust.",
  "numbers": "A September 2007 survey sponsored by the Institute of Medicine indicated that nearly 60 percent of respondents did not believe that the privacy of personal medical records and health information was adequately protected by federal and state laws and organizational practices. In April 2004, President Bush issued an executive order calling for widespread adoption of interoperable electronic health records within 10 years. In 2005, HHS awarded four health IT contracts that included requirements for developing solutions to comply with federal privacy requirements and identifying techniques and standards for securing health information. In January 2007, four test network implementations demonstrated potential nationwide health information exchange. HHS awarded contracts to nine health information exchange organizations and cooperative agreements to six additional organizations to develop trial implementations. The Secretary released a federal health IT strategic plan in June 2008, and the Office of the National Coordinator expected to publish a confidentiality, privacy, and security framework by December 2008. One strategy in the plan was to address inconsistent statutes or regulations for the exchange of electronic health information by the end of 2011. The State-Level Health Information Exchange Consensus Project issued a report in February 2007 and another report in March 2008. The Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security Workgroup submitted recommendations related to the notice principle in February and April 2008. The State Alliance for e-Health's information protection task force proposed five recommendations in August 2007. The audit was conducted from April 2008 through September 2008.",
  "recommended": "The report recommends that the Secretary of Health and Human Services direct the National Coordinator for Health IT to include in the department's overall privacy approach a process for assessing and prioritizing its many privacy-related initiatives and the needs of stakeholders, to ensure that key privacy principles and challenges are fully and adequately addressed. HHS generally agreed with the information in the report but neither agreed nor disagreed with this recommendation.",
  "unsettled": "The document states that HHS has not fully implemented an overall privacy approach and that more work remains. It notes that HHS has not defined a process for ensuring that all privacy principles and challenges will be fully and adequately addressed, so some principles and challenges may receive extensive attention while others may receive inadequate attention. Recommendations from the Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security Workgroup and the National Committee on Vital and Health Statistics were still under consideration by the Secretary. The confidentiality, privacy, and security framework was expected to be developed and published by the end of calendar year 2008 but had not yet been completed as of the report. HHS's written comments also caution that the report lists representative examples of HHS initiatives and is not intended to provide a complete compilation of HHS's privacy and security activities.",
